t: Ovary and fallopian tube: cysts, adnexal masses and tumors
sub: Sort an adnexal mass by age, ultrasound and marker, then name the ovarian cell it came from and the way it behaves.

pretest.q: Which ovarian neoplasm is most common in women under 30?
pretest.why: The mature cystic teratoma, or dermoid cyst, is the most common ovarian neoplasm in young women. It is benign, holds tissue from all three germ layers such as hair, teeth and sebum, and its weight makes the ovary prone to torsion.

w.Serous carcinoma: Serous carcinoma is the most common malignant ovarian tumor overall, but it mainly affects women after menopause and BRCA carriers.
w.Granulosa cell tumor: Granulosa cell tumors are uncommon sex cord-stromal tumors, most often seen around or after menopause with estrogen effects such as bleeding.
w.Brenner tumor: Brenner tumors are uncommon, usually benign epithelial tumors of transitional-type cells, typically found incidentally in older women.

pretest.q: Which serum marker does a yolk sac tumor secrete?
pretest.why: Yolk sac tissue makes alpha-fetoprotein in the embryo, so a yolk sac tumor, a malignant germ cell tumor of girls and young women, raises serum AFP and shows glomerulus-like Schiller-Duval bodies.

w.Inhibin: Inhibin is made by granulosa cells, so it marks granulosa cell tumors, which are sex cord-stromal rather than germ cell tumors.
w.CA-125: CA-125 comes from coelomic-type epithelium and rises with epithelial ovarian cancers, especially high-grade serous carcinoma, and with benign pelvic conditions.
w.Lactate dehydrogenase: Lactate dehydrogenase is the marker of dysgerminoma, the ovarian counterpart of seminoma, which grows as sheets of clear cells.

pretest.q: In ovarian torsion, which vessels are compressed first?
pretest.why: Veins and lymphatics have thin walls and low pressure, so twisting collapses them first while arterial blood keeps entering. The ovary swells with congestion and edema before arterial flow stops and infarction follows.

w.Ovarian artery: The ovarian artery has a thick muscular wall and high pressure, so it keeps delivering blood until swelling and further twisting finally occlude it.
w.Uterine artery: The uterine artery supplies the uterus and anastomoses with the ovarian artery, but it is not the vessel twisted in the infundibulopelvic ligament.
w.Internal iliac artery: The internal iliac artery lies on the pelvic sidewall far from the twisting pedicle, so torsion does not compress it.

body: Is an adnexal mass a cyst of ovulation or a true tumor?

The adnexa are the ovary, the fallopian tube and the tissue around them, so an adnexal mass is not always ovarian. A hydrosalpinx (a tube swollen with fluid after salpingitis), a tubo-ovarian abscess, a paratubal cyst and an ectopic pregnancy can all form a mass, so a pregnancy test comes first in any woman of reproductive age. Most ovarian masses in young women are **functional** cysts, exaggerations of the normal cycle rather than neoplasms. A {{rp15_folcyst|follicular cyst}}, the most common, forms when a follicle fails to rupture and keeps filling with fluid. A **corpus luteum cyst** forms after ovulation and can bleed, causing pain or rupture with blood in the pelvis. **Theca lutein cysts** are usually bilateral and multiloculated; very high hCG from a molar pregnancy, twins or ovarian hyperstimulation overstimulates the theca cells, and the cysts regress once hCG falls.

Transvaginal ultrasound is the first test. It shows the uterus with its endometrial stripe and each ovary with its follicles, and it sorts masses by risk. A thin-walled, anechoic simple cyst is almost always benign, so a young woman needs only expectant management, often with a repeat scan after a cycle or two, when a functional cyst has usually resolved. **Solid** components, **papillary projections**, thick **septations**, blood flow inside solid areas and ascites suggest malignancy. Rule-based systems such as the IOTA Simple Rules and O-RADS turn these features into a risk category. Age changes the list: in a prepubertal girl a solid mass is most often a germ cell tumor, and after menopause a complex mass is epithelial cancer until proven otherwise, so a postmenopausal woman with a complex mass, a raised CA-125 or ascites is referred to a gynecologic oncologist.
Germ cell tumors (dermoid, yolk sac, dysgerminoma); torsion
Ultrasound with AFP, hCG and LDH
Functional cysts, endometrioma, dermoid, ectopic pregnancy, hydrosalpinx
Epithelial carcinoma until proven otherwise; fibroma, granulosa tumor

CA-125 comes from coelomic-type epithelium, so endometriosis, fibroids, pelvic infection, pregnancy and even menstruation raise it. In a premenopausal woman a high value is therefore **nonspecific**, and it stays normal in about half of early-stage cancers. It helps most in a postmenopausal woman with a complex mass and for following a known epithelial cancer.
Why does an enlarged ovary twist, and what dies first?

In ovarian **torsion** the ovary rotates on the infundibulopelvic (suspensory) ligament, which carries the ovarian artery and vein, and on the utero-ovarian ligament. A heavy ovary, most often one enlarged by a dermoid or a cyst of 5 cm or more, is the usual lever, although a normal ovary can twist in a girl. The story is sudden, severe, one-sided pelvic pain with nausea and vomiting. Because veins and lymphatics have thin walls and low pressure, they collapse first while the thicker artery keeps pumping blood in, so the ovary swells with **venous** congestion and edema before arterial flow stops and **hemorrhagic infarction** follows. Doppler flow can persist early, so normal flow does not rule torsion out.
How torsion destroys an ovary, step by step
An ovary enlarged by a dermoid or cyst swings on its ligaments and twists the infundibulopelvic ligament that carries its vessels.
Low-pressure, thin-walled veins and lymphatics are squeezed shut while arterial blood still enters, so the ovary becomes congested and edematous.
Rising tissue pressure and further twisting finally stop arterial inflow, which is why an early Doppler study can still show flow.
Without inflow the ovary infarcts; prompt laparoscopic detorsion, even of a dark, swollen ovary, usually preserves ovarian function.
Which cell did the tumor come from?

Ovarian tumors are classified by the normal cell they resemble, because each of the ovary's three cell types keeps its own behavior when it becomes neoplastic. **Surface epithelium** (Müllerian-type epithelium of the ovary and fallopian tube) gives rise to about 90 percent of malignant tumors, mostly in older women. **Germ cells** give rise to teratomas and the other germ cell tumors, the common ovarian neoplasms of girls and young women. **Sex cord**-stromal cells (granulosa, theca, Sertoli and Leydig cells and fibroblasts) give rise to tumors that often make hormones. Metastases form a fourth group, such as the {{rp15_kruk|Krukenberg tumor}}: bilateral ovarian masses filled with mucin-secreting signet-ring cells, usually from a gastric primary.

Epithelial tumors run from benign to borderline to malignant. **Serous** tumors are the most common, both benign and malignant; they are often bilateral, and their carcinomas contain concentric calcified psammoma bodies. **Mucinous** tumors can grow very large and are usually unilateral; KRAS mutation is typical, and bilateral mucinous masses suggest metastasis from the appendix or gut. Pseudomyxoma peritonei, a belly full of gelatinous mucin, usually comes from an appendiceal tumor rather than the ovary. Endometrioid and clear cell carcinomas arise from endometriosis, and endometrioid tumors also occur in Lynch syndrome. The **Brenner tumor**, made of transitional-type nests with coffee-bean nuclei, is usually benign. A {{rp15_bord|borderline tumor}} shows epithelial stratification and atypia without destructive stromal invasion, and its peritoneal implants are usually noninvasive, so most patients do well.

Carcinomas follow two paths. Type I carcinomas (low-grade serous, mucinous, endometrioid and clear cell) grow slowly and step by step from borderline tumors or endometriosis, driven by KRAS, BRAF or PTEN changes. Type II is **high-grade serous carcinoma**, the most common and most lethal ovarian cancer. It starts as {{rp15_stic|serous tubal intraepithelial carcinoma}} in the fimbriated end of the fallopian tube, carries an early TP53 mutation, and is the ovarian cancer of BRCA1 and BRCA2 carriers. It spreads by shedding cells onto peritoneal surfaces, so women present late with vague bloating, early satiety and rising abdominal girth from ascites and **omental** caking. Treatment is surgical staging with cytoreductive (debulking) surgery and platinum-based chemotherapy, with PARP inhibitors for BRCA carriers.
TP53 in nearly all; often BRCA1 or BRCA2
Slow; often confined to the ovary
Why do oral contraceptives and tubal surgery lower ovarian cancer risk?

Each ovulation breaks the ovarian surface and bathes the nearby fimbriae in follicular fluid full of inflammatory mediators, and the repair needs cell division that can copy DNA errors. Anything that cuts the lifetime number of ovulations, such as oral contraceptives, pregnancy and breastfeeding, therefore lowers risk, while nulliparity, early menarche and late menopause raise it. Tubal ligation and salpingectomy protect for a second reason: most high-grade serous carcinomas begin in the fimbriated tube, so removing or isolating the tube removes the cells that start the cancer. That is why salpingectomy is offered during other pelvic surgery.
No screening test works for average-risk women

Large trials of yearly CA-125 and transvaginal ultrasound did not lower ovarian cancer deaths, and false positives led to needless surgery, so the USPSTF recommends against screening women at average risk. Prevention targets high-risk women instead: BRCA carriers are offered risk-reducing salpingo-oophorectomy once childbearing is complete.
Which tumors announce themselves with a marker or a hormone?

Germ cell tumors are named for the tissue they imitate. The mature cystic **teratoma**, or dermoid cyst, is the most common ovarian neoplasm in young women; it holds hair, teeth and sebum from all three germ layers, it is benign, and its weight makes torsion likely. Struma ovarii is a teratoma made mostly of thyroid tissue that can cause hyperthyroidism, while an immature teratoma contains immature neuroepithelium and is malignant. The **dysgerminoma**, the ovarian counterpart of seminoma, forms sheets of large clear cells with lymphocyte-rich septa, raises lactate dehydrogenase (LDH), is very radiosensitive, and is more common in dysgenetic gonads that carry Y material (Swyer syndrome, some Turner mosaics). The **yolk sac tumor** of girls and young women makes alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) and shows glomerulus-like {{rp15_sd|Schiller-Duval bodies}}, and choriocarcinoma makes human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG) from trophoblast without villi.

Sex cord-stromal tumors act like the cells they came from. The **granulosa cell tumor** makes estrogen: in a young girl it causes precocious puberty, and in an older woman it causes endometrial hyperplasia, endometrial cancer and postmenopausal bleeding. Its cells have grooved coffee-bean nuclei around small follicle-like {{rp15_ce|Call-Exner bodies}}, and inhibin is its serum marker. The **Sertoli-Leydig cell tumor** makes androgens, so a young woman develops hirsutism, a deeper voice and clitoromegaly. The thecoma makes estrogen, and the fibroma makes no hormone but can cause **Meigs syndrome**: an ovarian fibroma with ascites and a right pleural effusion, all of which resolve once the tumor is removed.

body.q: A 19-year-old has a solid ovarian mass and a markedly raised serum AFP. Which reasoning best identifies the tumor?
o: AFP is made by epithelial ovarian cancers, so the mass is most likely a serous carcinoma
A raised marker means hormone production, so the tumor must come from sex cord-stromal cells
AFP comes from trophoblast, so the mass is most likely a choriocarcinoma that also makes hCG
AFP is a yolk sac protein, so a germ cell tumor imitating yolk sac is most likely
body.why: Each germ cell tumor secretes the protein of the tissue it imitates. Embryonic yolk sac makes alpha-fetoprotein, so a yolk sac tumor raises AFP and shows Schiller-Duval bodies. Trophoblast makes hCG, so choriocarcinoma raises hCG instead, and dysgerminoma raises LDH. Epithelial cancers raise CA-125, and sex cord-stromal tumors make steroid hormones and inhibin rather than a fetal protein. Her age fits too, because germ cell tumors are the malignant ovarian tumors of girls and young women.
